claims.text: High-purity copper exhibits superior ductility compared with many other metals.
The superior ductility of high-purity copper is due to its FCC crystal structure.
High-purity annealed copper has a well-recrystallized FCC structure.
The FCC lattice in copper provides multiple active slip systems.
Copper's FCC structure provides a high density of slip planes.
The available slip planes facilitate extensive dislocation motion under tensile stress.
Extensive dislocation motion enables substantial plastic deformation and produces high ductility.
At room temperature, copper samples will undergo extensive plastic deformation before fracture in tensile testing.
At room temperature, copper samples will exhibit high elongation before fracture.
BCC metals such as pure iron in its BCC phase are less ductile than high-purity annealed copper under similar conditions.
Significant impurities may reduce the ductility of copper.
Testing far below room temperature may reduce copper's ductility because dislocation mobility becomes limited.
The magnitude of copper's proposed ductility advantage and its sensitivity to impurity content and microstructure are not quantified.
Failure of high-purity copper to show significantly greater elongation or strain before fracture than the BCC comparator under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
